lesson.title: Figures of repetition and balance

steps.headline: Repeating an opening and matching opposites both give a sentence a frame to hold on to.

lead.text: Anaphora repeats a word or phrase at the start of successive clauses, so attention moves to what changes inside the frame. Antithesis places opposed ideas in parallel grammatical form, so the parallel sharpens the opposition.
Dickens opens A Tale of Two Cities with one sentence that keeps a single frame going for ten clauses. Here is its start. Count how often the frame opens a clause.

reveal.text: Four times in this extract. The repeated opening is anaphora: the frame stays still while best and worst, wisdom and foolishness change inside it. Douglass uses “your” the same way, and each repetition points back at his audience.

model.source: Dickens, A Tale of Two Cities, opening

lead.text: Lincoln sets two halves in one grammatical frame. Only the opposed words change.

reveal.text: The matching frame makes the opposition collide, so the speech enacts its own modesty: words matter less than deeds. Dickens's “best” and “worst” sit in the same slot of the same clause.

steps.headline: Name the figure in Lincoln's “what we say here” against “what they did here”.

workedSteps.text: Put the two halves side by side: “what we say here” and “what they did here”.
The grammar is identical. Only the words change: “we” against “they”, saying against doing.
Name the figure that balances opposed ideas in parallel form.

spans.text: The world will little note, nor long remember

model.source: Dickens, A Tale of Two Cities, opening

steps.headline: Chiasmus reverses its terms, and a tricolon runs three members in step.

lead.text: Chiasmus repeats terms in reverse order, A B then B A. Lines drawn between the matching words cross like the Greek letter chi. When the same words return it is strictly antimetabole. A tricolon is a series of three parallel members.
Douglass places this at the turning point of his Narrative, just before he fights back against Covey. The grammar reverses as his life does. Look at the order of the terms in each half.

reveal.text: The terms return reversed: man, slave, then slave, man. Because the same words come back, the stricter name is antimetabole.

lead.text: Lincoln's close varies only the preposition: “of the people, by the people, for the people”. Each phrase adds a relation: government drawn from the people, run by them, serving them.

reveal.text: Three parallel members make a tricolon. His earlier verbs, “dedicate”, “consecrate” and “hallow”, climb from civic to sacred, so those members grow in weight.

lesson.orientation: Recognise anaphora, antithesis, chiasmus and tricolon in Dickens, Lincoln, Douglass and Shakespeare. Say what each figure does to an argument.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh text after a delay.

blocks.text: Caesar's report of a victory is remembered in English as three short parts.

intro.promise: By the end you'll recognise four figures of repetition and balance and say what each does to an argument.

recap.keyIdea: Figures of repetition and balance give an argument shape. Each one tells the reader where to look: at what changes, what is opposed, what reverses.

blocks.text: You counted four “it was” openings in Dickens and named Lincoln's “we” against “they” as antithesis. You also met Douglass's reversal of man and slave, and Lincoln's “of, by and for the people”.

recap.nextHook: Sentences have a sound as well as a shape. Next: metre, the beat under the words.

questions.prompt: Dickens opens A Tale of Two Cities: 'It was the best of times, it was the worst of times, it was the age of wisdom, it was the age of foolishness.' How many times does 'it was' open a clause in this extract?
hints: Split the extract at each comma.
Mark the first two words of each clause.
Count the clauses that open the same way.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Four. The repeated opening is anaphora; in the full sentence Dickens keeps it going for ten clauses.

questions.onCorrect: Four. The repeated opening is anaphora, and Dickens keeps it going for ten clauses in the full sentence.

misconceptions.feedback: That is how long the full sentence keeps the frame going. Count only the extract shown.
Look again: one more clause opens the same way.
Mark the first two words of every clause, not just the first pair.
Count only the clauses that open with the repeated words.

questions.prompt: Lincoln sets 'what we say here' against 'what they did here' in matching grammatical form. Name the figure that balances opposed ideas in parallel structure.
hints: The Greek name means 'setting against'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Antithesis: contrasting ideas placed in parallel form, here saying against doing and 'we' against 'they'.

questions.onCorrect: Antithesis: opposed ideas, saying against doing and “we” against “they”, in matching grammatical form.

misconceptions.feedback: Chiasmus reverses the order of terms. Here the frame stays the same and the words oppose.
Anaphora is repetition at the start of clauses. The point here is the opposition inside a matching frame.

questions.prompt: Douglass: 'You have seen how a man was made a slave; you shall see how a slave was made a man.' The terms return in reverse order, A B B A. Name the figure.
hints: The name comes from the Greek letter chi, shaped like an X.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Chiasmus (strictly antimetabole, since the same words return): A B, then B A.

questions.onCorrect: Chiasmus (strictly antimetabole, since the same words return): A B, then B A.

misconceptions.feedback: The ideas do oppose, but what defines this figure is that the order of terms reverses.
Nothing repeats at the start of clauses. Look at the order of the terms in each half.

questions.prompt: 'Government of the people, by the people, for the people.' Name the figure made of three parallel members.
hints: The Greek prefix for three is joined to the word for a clause or limb.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A tricolon: three parallel members, here three prepositional phrases sharing one noun.

questions.onCorrect: A tricolon: three parallel members, here three prepositional phrases sharing one noun.

misconceptions.feedback: Anaphora repeats an opening word. The question asks about the three-part pattern itself.
Nothing is set against anything here. Count the parallel members.

questions.prompt: Douglass: 'your celebration is a sham; your boasted liberty, an unholy license; your national greatness, swelling vanity.' Which figure does the repeated opening 'your' create?
hints: Repetition at the start of successive clauses has a name from the Greek for 'carrying back'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Anaphora: repetition at the start of successive clauses, here pointing each charge at the audience.

questions.onCorrect: Anaphora: repetition at the start of successive clauses, here pointing each charge at the audience.

misconceptions.feedback: The series does run to three, but the figure the repeated opening creates is a different one.
The charges are not set against opposites. Look at how each clause begins.

questions.prompt: The witches in Macbeth chant 'Fair is foul, and foul is fair.' Which figure is this?
hints: Look at the order of the two repeated words in each half.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Chiasmus: fair, foul / foul, fair. The reversal suits a play in which appearances invert.

questions.onCorrect: Chiasmus: fair, foul, then foul, fair. The reversal suits a play in which appearances invert.

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing repeats at the start of clauses here. Check the order of the two words in each half.
There is no series of three members. Look at how the two repeated words are ordered.

questions.prompt: “I came, I saw, I conquered.” How many of its parts begin with “I”?
hints: Split the line at each comma.
Look at the first word of each part.
Count the parts that open with the same word.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three: each of the three short parts begins with “I”.

questions.onCorrect: Three. Starting every part the same way makes the sentence move like a march.

misconceptions.feedback: Check each part of the line, not only the first.
There is one more part after the second comma.
Count the parts that begin with the word, not the word itself wherever it appears.

questions.prompt: In “Every day, every hour, every minute”, which word repeats at the start of each part?
hints: Compare the first word of each part.
questions.onCorrect: “Every” opens each part. Repeating the opening word is anaphora, and it draws the eye to what changes.

misconceptions.feedback: Those are the parts that change. Find the word that stays the same each time.

questions.prompt: “Never let a fool kiss you or a kiss fool you.” In the second half, which of the two repeated words comes first?
hints: Compare the two halves. Which word leads in each?
questions.onCorrect: “Kiss” comes first in the second half, “fool” in the first. The terms return in reverse order: chiasmus.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the order of the first half. In the second half the order flips.

questions.prompt: Which line is built as an antithesis?
hints: Look for opposed ideas placed in parallel form.
